[SYSTEM] You are a Python ML engineer. Write a single, self-contained Python script that trains and evaluates the architecture from the proposal for the BirdCLEF 2026 multi-label task. ## Input tensor shape — READ THIS FIRST The data loader produces tensors of shape **(batch, 1, n_mels, time_frames)** — a 4-dimensional tensor, image-like. Typical values: (32, 1, 128, 313). This means: - Use `nn.Conv2d`, NOT `nn.Conv1d`. Conv1d only accepts 3D tensors (batch, channels, time) and will crash on 4D input. - Use `nn.MaxPool2d` / `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d`, not the 1D versions. - Treat each spectrogram as an image with 1 channel. ## Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d layers The FIRST Conv2d must have `in_channels=1` because the input has 1 channel. Every subsequent Conv2d's `in_channels` MUST equal the previous Conv2d's `out_channels`. A common LLM mistake is: self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # out: 64 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # WRONG: expects 1 channel, gets 64 The correct version: self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # out: 64 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3) # in=64 matches conv1 out=64 Before writing each Conv2d, think about what tensor flows into it and explicitly set `in_channels` to the previous layer's `out_channels`. If you are unsure, use `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))` to collapse the spatial dims and a `nn.Linear(out_channels, num_classes)` at the end — that guarantees the output dimension is correct regardless of input size. ## Architecture sources — TWO valid paths The proposal's `architecture` field tells you what to build: (A) REGISTRY MODEL — the `architecture` value matches a name in the Model Registry (e.g. "cnn_small_v1", "efficientnet_b0"): → Copy the registry's `import_snippet` VERBATIM. Use the EXACT capitalization shown there (e.g. `CnnSmallV1`, NOT `cnn_small_v1`). → Registry models are in `pipelines.models` or in `torchvision.models`. The snippet tells you which. Do NOT invent imports like `from torchvision.models import CnnSmallV1` — that is wrong; CnnSmallV1 lives in `pipelines.models`. (B) CUSTOM MODEL — the `architecture` describes a free-form design that is not a registry name (e.g. "ResNet-style 4-block CNN with SE attention"): → Define the full `nn.Module` class(es) inline. Everything must be imported from `torch`, `torch.nn`, `torchvision`, `torchaudio`, `sklearn`, `numpy`, or `pipelines`, OR defined within the script. → The final logit vector MUST have length `num_classes` (multi-label output). `num_classes` comes from `load_precomputed_dataset()` — do NOT hardcode 234 or any other number. WHY: on macOS (and Windows), the default multiprocessing start method is `spawn`. Without the `__main__` guard, every worker would re-run your training loop — which tries to spawn its own workers — and Python raises: RuntimeError: An attempt has been made to start a new process before the current process has finished its bootstrapping phase. You will see "device: mps / loading data... / model built..." printed over and over in the logs, followed by that RuntimeError. If that happens, you forgot the `__main__` guard. Do NOT use ResNet-50/101, EfficientNet-B4+, or any model with >10M parameters. - If in doubt, prefer fewer channels and fewer layers. ## Common PyTorch pitfalls that have crashed previous runs ### 0. `device.type` is a PROPERTY, not a method — NO parentheses `torch.device.type` is a plain string attribute: if device.type == 'cuda': # CORRECT if device.type == 'mps': # CORRECT Writing `device.type()` with parentheses causes: TypeError: 'str' object is not callable NEVER write `device.type()` — always use `device.type` (no parens). ### 0b. `nn.GRU` and `nn.LSTM` return TUPLES, not tensors `nn.GRU(...)` and `nn.LSTM(...)` return `(output, hidden_state)`, NOT a single tensor. You MUST unpack them: gru = nn.GRU(input_size=128, hidden_size=128, batch_first=True) output, hidden = gru(x) # CORRECT — unpack the tuple x = output # use the output tensor WRONG — calling tensor methods on the tuple: x = gru(x).permute(...) # AttributeError: 'tuple' has no 'permute' x = gru(x).transpose(...) # AttributeError: 'tuple' has no 'transpose' Always unpack: `output, _ = gru(x)` then operate on `output`. ### 1. `self.relu` vs `F.relu` — do NOT mix them up There are two correct ways to apply ReLU (or any other activation) in a PyTorch nn.Module. You must pick ONE per module and stick to it. WRONG (this is the #1 cause of AttributeError failures in our runs): class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) # forgot to define self.relu here! def forward(self, x): x = self.relu(self.conv1(x)) # AttributeError: no attribute 'relu' CORRECT option A — register the activation as a submodule: class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) # <-- defined in __init__ def forward(self, x): x = self.relu(self.conv1(x)) # works CORRECT option B — use the functional form (simpler, no __init__ line): import torch.nn.functional as F class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.conv1(x)) # works, no self.relu needed Rule of thumb: option B (`F.relu`) is simpler for stateless activations (relu, gelu, sigmoid, softmax). Use it unless you have a specific reason to need option A. Same applies to `F.max_pool2d`, `F.adaptive_avg_pool2d`, `F.dropout`, etc. ### 2. Shape mismatch on the flatten → linear boundary — USE LazyLinear A classic bug: after a stack of Conv2d + pooling, the spatial size of the feature map depends on the input. Writing `nn.Linear(2048, num_classes)` only works if the feature map's flattened size is exactly 2048. Change the input shape and it crashes with: RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x1600 and 2048x234) This is the #1 failure in our runs and the shape-arithmetic trick is hard to get right. So we REQUIRE a bullet-proof pattern that works regardless of the conv stack: **`nn.LazyLinear(num_classes)`**. `nn.LazyLinear` infers its `in_features` from the first forward pass, so you can NEVER write the wrong number. Use it like this: class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), ) self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)) # still a good idea self.head = nn.LazyLinear(num_classes) # ← no in_features! def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = self.pool(x).flatten(1) # collapses (B, C, 1, 1) → (B, C) return self.head(x) Rules for using `nn.LazyLinear`: - ONE `LazyLinear` call per model — for the classifier head. - The model MUST be moved to the device BEFORE the first forward pass so the lazy layer materializes on the right device. - **CRITICAL**: After `.to(device)`, you MUST run a dummy forward pass to initialize the lazy parameters BEFORE calling `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())`. Without this, `p.numel()` crashes with: ValueError: Attempted to use an uninitialized parameter Do this: model = MyModel(num_classes=num_classes).to(device) # Initialize lazy modules with a dummy forward pass with torch.no_grad(): dummy = torch.zeros(1, 1, 128, 313, device=device) model(dummy) n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) - Do NOT pass `in_features` to LazyLinear — it has no such arg. LazyLinear removes this whole class of bugs — prefer it. ### 3. Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d (already covered above) Each Conv2d's `in_channels` MUST equal the previous Conv2d's `out_channels`. See the "Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d layers" section. ## Variable scoping reminder Define `num_classes` at module scope — it comes from load_precomputed_dataset and you will use it to instantiate the model. Do NOT put it inside a function and then try to use it from the outside — that causes NameError. Likewise, do NOT build a `hyperparams` dict and then look things up from it (`hyperparams["augmentation"]`) — just use the values directly. import json
import os
import time
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, f1_score
from pipelines.data_loader import load_precomputed_dataset, compute_pos_weight

# === Device selection (READ from env var — do NOT hardcode) ===
DEVICE_NAME = os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_DEVICE", "cpu")
device = torch.device(DEVICE_NAME)

# === Hardcode hyperparameters from the proposal (NOT a hyperparams dict) ===
# Read epochs from environment variable, default to 1 for quick runs.
EPOCHS = int(os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_EPOCHS", "1"))
LR = 1e-3
# Augmentation dictionary is passed directly to the data loader
AUGMENTATION = {"time_shift": True, "noise_injection": True}

# === Registry Model Import ===
# The backbone uses cnn_small_v1
try:
    from pipelines.models import CnnSmallV1
except ImportError:
    print("Error: Could not import CnnSmallV1 from pipelines.models. Ensure the environment is set up correctly.", flush=True)
    raise

# === Model definition at MODULE scope ===
class CnnGruHybridModel(nn.Module):
